explanation: Lafcadio Hearn used tsunami, Japanese for harbour wave, in an 1897 book about Japan. Teenager, at first spelled teen-ager, turns up only in the 1920s.

claims.text: 'Tsunami' was in English use by 1897, when Lafcadio Hearn used it in Gleanings in Buddha-Fields.
'Teenager' is first recorded in the 1920s, in the hyphenated form 'teen-ager'.
Japanese tsunami means 'harbour wave', from tsu, 'harbour', and nami, 'wave'.

writerNotes: Counterintuitive: tsunami became familiar to most people only after 2004, so they assume it is the newer word; it is older by about 25 years. Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. The selfCheck field itself is left out because the CNT-1 item schema refuses it as an unknown key, so the codes are recorded here. lint: content:check reports no errors and no warnings for this item. claims: 3 listed, 3 high (date, etymology) and 0 standard, every one at or above the C26 floor and raised where a fact is beyond everyday knowledge. datasets: no pinned dataset covers word histories. rivalTest: Value b is stored as 1922, the earliest date I know for teen-ager; a later first use of either spelling only widens the gap. An earlier English use of tsunami (some cite 1896) only widens it too. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: both words are used in every variety of English. style: Oxford spelling, straight single quotes, plain hyphens only, explanation of 25 words. myths: every claim screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a practice item. doubts: none.
